title: Lira and the Whispering Mountain Myths
markdown:
The air above the Whispering Mountains tasted thin, like starlight that had been left out overnight. Observatories sat on the treeline like metal owls, unblinking, glass eyes aimed at weather that had not yet decided to arrive. Lira lived in one of them, an elf whose mind ran to neat plans and exact calculations. She would not leave a room without knowing how many steps the corridor took, and how much energy each step spent. Her boots stood in a line. Her pencils stood in a line. The mountains, unfortunately, did not.

Tinker, her marmot, was the colour of a biscuit with a dash of cinnamon. He was not a pet so much as a furry conscience. Wet nose when she drifted. A chitter when she aimed herself at mountain gorse. His routes were shorter than her maps, which irritated her in a way she enjoyed. He had a way of sitting on the corner of a chart as if he were a paperweight with opinions.

The mule train was late. Star-charts. A brand-new extra-shiny telescope lens. The usual promises of astronomical discovery, stacked on panniers that had not appeared. Lira smoothed maps creased from many journeys, checked the observatory’s forecast crystals, and drew a neat straight line from home to the supply depot just over the ridge. Simple, really. She packed extra nuts for Tinker. One can never have too many snacks on an adventure, even a sensible one.

Crag’s End, nestled in a hollow where the wind pretended to be polite, did not believe in simple. Faces pale. Hands wrung with a worry that sounded suspiciously like excitement.

“You can’t go that way, Lira. That’s the Dragon’s Shadow Path. Cursed. Only the foolish or the foolhardy.”

They spoke of ancient dragons slumbering under the peaks, dreams so powerful they shaped the winds into treacherous gusts and made the rocks tremble. An elf, even a sensible one, with a mule and a timetable, would surely disturb that fiery sleep.

Lira, whose sharp eyes could spot a falling star from fifty miles and whose ears could hear a pixie sneeze in a hurricane, found this tiresome.

“Dragons? The only thing I expect to disturb is a particularly grumpy marmot if we don’t hurry and get those star-charts. And Tinker is rarely grumpy before elevenses.”

Tinker, meticulously grooming his whiskers, gave an indignant squeak, as if to say he was always ready for elevenses.

Still they were adamant. They insisted on a longer, winding, frankly inefficient route, blessed, they said, by the spirits of ancient mountain goats who had once outsmarted a grumpy troll. Old Bessie the weaver clutched a half-finished sock.

“It’s the legends, Lira. They have a way of being true, even when they don’t make a lick of sense.”

Lira’s sigh was more exasperation than despair. She went to seek a creature known for straightforwardness, even if that creature was a bit of an ogre. She went to Grok.

Grok the baker was green, hulking, and could crush boulders into pebbles with a casual squeeze, which he never did to dough. He kneaded as if pastry might bruise. If he said his cloud-cakes—so light they practically floated—would be ready at dawn, they were ready when the first sunbeam kissed the highest peak. Punctual, for an ogre. His pastries were the stuff of legend themselves, which Lira tried not to hold against them.

She found him in a cavernous bakery inside the mountain. Cinnamon. Caramelised sugar. Something vaguely volcanic: magma muffins, probably.

“Grok,” she said, holding her neatly folded map, “the observatory needs those supplies. Crag’s End is insisting on a terribly long detour through the Whispering Pass. They claim it’s haunted by dragons.”

Grok dusted flour from an enormous checkered apron and let out a rumbling chuckle that shook the stalactites.

“Dragons, eh? My Aunt Griselda always said she heard them grumbling when she was a girl. Sounded like a thousand boulders tumbling down a very deep well. Unsettling, I imagine.” He scratched an enormous bumpy head. “But that path is also where old Silas, the shepherd from the south slope, lost his prize sheep last spring. Went right over the edge, they said, with a most frightful bleat. Best stick to the longer route, Lira. Better safe than sorry. And who wants to be sorry when they could be eating a perfectly good pastry?”

Lira felt a familiar prickle, an itch she could not reach.

“But Grok, the direct path is perfectly safe. A well-worn mule track, used by traders for generations. The legends are stories. Tall tales from people with too much time and not enough sense.”

“Stories have roots, Lira.” He shaped a fluffy muffin with practiced ease. “And sometimes those roots grow into trouble. Especially when they involve dragons. I’ll be delivering these pastries to the mountain shrine at noon. If you haven’t got your supplies by then, and you’re still dithering about dragon paths, I can’t help you any further. My schedule is as rigid as a well-baked loaf.”

Wouldn’t you know it: Lira found herself later at the entrance to the very pass the villagers feared. Tinker scampered ahead, nose twitching with curiosity, not fear. The path was well-trodden, not by scaly claws but by generations of goats and sturdy mules. As they rounded a bend, Lira nearly stumbled over a large slumped form. An ogre, back to them, head bent, watching a flock of shaggy mountain goats the colour of storm clouds. Burr, Grok’s cousin, known more for quiet silences than sharp insights. He seemed to blend into the rocks, another craggy outcrop.

Lira hesitated. Burr spent his days with the flock. He was closer to the ground than the fearful villagers.

“Excuse me. Have you seen anything unusual on this path recently? Anything that might cause alarm?”

Burr turned slowly. Eyes surprisingly bright, keenly observant. He surveyed Lira, then Tinker, then the path ahead. He did not speak for a long moment. Lira felt a pang of doubt. Perhaps he was only another simple-minded ogre. Then he pointed a massive gnarled finger toward a narrow, almost invisible track branching off the main path, up a steep rocky incline.

“Goats.”

Lira blinked. “Goats? But the legends speak of dragons.”

“Mm.” His gaze stayed on the flock. “They like the high places. And the sun. And when they shift their weight on the scree, or rub against the hollow rocks, they make a rumbling sound. Like rocks falling. Like distant thunder.” A chin-gesture at the main path. “This path is old. Used by many. But the ones who talk of dragons don’t look closely. They hear the rumbling, and they imagine the ancient ones, sleeping and dreaming. They forget the little ones, the bleating ones, who just want to find the best patch of moss.”

Lira looked at the faint goat trail, then at the imposing Dragon’s Shadow Path. Burr’s words clicked like cut gears. Dragon’s breath: wind whistling through hollowed rock. Rumbling: Burr’s own herds shifting. The village had built its terrifying legends on livestock and the mountain’s ordinary noises.

“You mean there are no dragons here at all?”

Burr shrugged, a movement that rippled his frame like a landslide. “Only goats who like sunbathing on warm rocks. And the wind, which can sound like anything if you listen hard enough. And very patient shepherds who know the difference between a grumble and a bleat.”

As if timed by something other than spirits, a bell clanged up the mountainside, cheerful and purposeful. With it, on the crisp air, freshly baked pastry. At the mouth of the pass, silhouetted against afternoon, stood Grok and his laden cart. His timing, as always, was impeccable.

“Pastries,” Lira said, and a laugh got out of her. “And supplies.” She hurried. Tinker zipped. Burr lumbered respectfully behind. She told Grok what the quiet shepherd had shown her. The villagers, gathered in the square, half-expecting a puff of smoke, watched her return with a telescope lens and a cart of cloud-cakes.

She held the lens up. It caught a scrap of afternoon and threw it, small and ordinary, onto the cobbles. She did not lecture them about open eyes. She nodded at Burr, who offered a shy, almost imperceptible nod of his own.

Grok, seeing an excellent opportunity for timed generosity, began handing out warm fluffy cakes. Sweet steam. Fear going soggy at the edges. As the sun dipped, Lira sat with Tinker, the lens stowed, watching moonlight silver the frost on Crag’s End. Someone was still chewing. Burr’s goats, somewhere above, shifted their weight, and the mountain made the sound it had always made. Lira closed her map without folding it first, which, for her, was the whole of the change. The observatory’s metal owl of a dome waited. The stars, when they came, would not care whether anyone had believed in dragons.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for teens
